title: Notation and Conventions
about: The single source for the project's notation and conventions. scripts/build_notation.py generates Aim/Common/Notation.tex from this file, and scripts/check_conventions.py enforces the rules marked enforced. Standard mathematical notation is not listed. The deviations table holds only the places where the Lean is written differently from standard mathematics; add a row when a Lean file first needs one.

naming.about: How declarations are named. This is a summary, in this project's words and with this project's examples where it has one, of the Lean standard library and Mathlib naming conventions, kept here so they can be read without leaving the repository. The two documents under References are the authority. Checked against them on 2026-11-24.

patterns.meaning: A name spells out the conclusion of the theorem, reading its symbols left to right with the dictionary above.
Hypotheses follow the conclusion, each introduced by `of`, in the order they appear. A → B → C is named `C_of_A_of_B`. A hypothesis that is obvious from the conclusion is left out.
patterns.example: `le_of_add_le_add_right` concludes a ≤ b from a + c ≤ b + c

patterns.meaning: The statement is an `↔`. A longer form `A_iff_B` names both sides.
Restates a definition so that it can be unfolded by name.
a R a, with `a` given explicitly for `refl` and found by Lean for `rfl`; `irrefl` is ¬ a R a.
a R b → b R a; a R b → b R c → a R c; a R b → b R a → a = b.
f a b = f b a; f (f a b) c = f a (f b c). Compare `symm`, which is about a relation, not an operation.
a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c; (a + b) * c = a * c + b * c.
Tells apart the two symmetric versions of a theorem. It usually names the side that varies.
`cancel` is f a = f b → a = b, or g (f a) = a. `inj` is the two-way form f a = f b ↔ a = b.
a ≤ b → f a ≤ f b.
`T.ext`: two objects of type `T` that agree on every element, or every argument, are equal. `T.ext_iff` is the two-way form.
A variable appears more than once in the conclusion.
Used in place of `zero_lt`, `lt_zero`, `zero_le`, `le_zero`. A nonzero element is `ne_zero`, never `nonzero`.

patterns.pattern: le and lt, ge and gt
patterns.meaning: Statements are written with ≤ and <, never ≥ and >. A name uses `le` and `lt` for the first such relation; `ge` and `gt` appear only to say that a later relation has its two sides the other way round.
patterns.example: `lt_iff_le_not_ge` is a < b ↔ a ≤ b ∧ ¬ b ≤ a

patterns.meaning: A name follows the order in which the statement is written.
A theorem whose main hypothesis is a statement `P …` is placed in the namespace `P`, so that from `h : P …` it can be written `h.name`.
A property named by a noun begins with `Is`. A property named by an adjective need not. `Has` is used when the property says that something else exists.
The property comes first, in lowerCamelCase, then what it is about.
A principle that proves a statement for every element is named `induction`. One that builds an object for every element is named `rec`.
Two versions of a theorem are told apart by a describing word, not by a trailing `'`.
Names use American spelling. Comments and prose may use any standard spelling.

local.lean: the standard library recommends `_iff`; Mathlib drops it when the short name is free (`mem_union`)
local.here: every `↔` lemma has `iff` in its name
local.why: one rule, and the short name stays free for the one-way fact

local.lean: `α`, `β` for a general type; a mathematical letter where the type has a role
local.here: `X`, `Y` for a general type; `F`, `R`, `N` by role
a major concept with an abbreviated Lean name also has a full name; see Names
local.why: the statements should read as mathematics

local.here: every theorem states its type arguments itself, first
local.why: each statement can be read on its own

rules.statement: Declarations are named by the Lean and Mathlib naming conventions, as summarised under Naming, with the local differences listed there.
A theorem whose statement is an `↔` has `iff` in its name.
A theorem states its type arguments itself, first, as in `theorem name {X : Type u}`, and does not rely on a `variable` line for them.
A major concept has a readable full name. Where its Lean name is abbreviated, the Lean name is the definition and the full name is an `abbrev` for it. Lemmas have one name, after the Lean name.
Every theorem, lemma, corollary, proposition and example is proved with a `by` tactic block, so that the proof can be stepped through in the InfoView.
A file that only re-exports its folder is named <Folder>Aggregator.lean and contains imports and a module docstring, no declarations.
Mathematics is declared in `namespace Aim`. A sub-namespace exists only when it is the name of a type and holds that type's own operations.

rules.statement: A file under Aim/ imports the interface files it needs, never the root module `Aim`, which also brings in every construction.
Nothing under Aim/ or tests/ imports Mathlib. Mathlib appears only in validation/mathlib.
A variable that is a set, a collection or a family of sets is an uppercase letter. An element of a set is a lowercase letter.
Subtraction and division on a field are the derived operations. A construction of a number system never defines its own.
A proof cites the lemmas of an interface (membership lemmas for sets, the two equations for `recurse`) and does not unfold its definitions.
A `sorry` marks a proof still to be written by the learner. It is never a defect.
